findings.title: The board and the local app now publish different files for the same run: the collector calls run_doc without the repository, so every in-repo edit reads site/index.html on the board but …/index.html locally, breaking AC-64 equal records, and the local equivalence tests cannot see it

evidence.value: repo_of = {p[id]: p[repoPath] for p in st[projects]}; derive.run_doc(r, i, pid, repo_of.get(pid))
docs[run][r[id]] = derive.run_doc(r, i, st[project_of].get(sid)) with no repo argument; st[projects] is in hand at collector.py:439, so the fix is one dict and one argument.
run_doc docstring: without a repo every absolute path is published as …/ and its file name.
Edited paths inside repoPath that would differ between board and local: 56 occurrences for dispatch-board and 110 for platform-catalogue. The divergence affects most builder runs, not an edge case.

No Edit, Write, MultiEdit or NotebookEdit tool call in any fixture: test_conformance.py builds only Agent (:112), TaskStop (:116) and Skill (:171-172, :304-305) calls, and test_collector.py reuses the exporter test tree basic() fixture, which has no edits. assert_equivalent (test_collector.py:45-46) therefore compares run records with no files key on either side; 304 OK is vacuous for this field. Confirmed.

The collector shall produce session, run and project records equal to the exporter documents; whichever of PBI-019 and a feature PBI lands second extends this fixture. PBI-014 is that second-landing feature PBI, but local/** is outside its allowed_areas.

The divergence withholds rather than leaks: local shows less and publishes no absolute path. No observer today: PBI-007 (log-on deployment) is In Progress in its own worktree at 560e296 with its scheduled tasks unregistered, although the merged collector and server can still be run by hand.

findings.impact: Once merged, main violates an approved invariant (FR-87 / AC-64 and the spec decision behind it) for every run that edited a file inside its repository. The test meant to guard it passes only because its fixtures never edit a file. Nobody sees it until the local app is deployed or run by hand, and the difference is conservative; the real risk is the fix being forgotten until PBI-007 ships a local board that silently disagrees with the published one.
findings.remediation: Recommended disposition (b), made enforceable rather than a note. Before merge, the orchestrator records a follow-up PBI whose allowed_areas include local/collector.py and local/tests/**. That PBI builds repo_of from st[projects] and passes repo_of.get(pid) at collector.py:436, and extends the AC-64 equivalence fixture with an in-repo edit, an outside-repo write and a worktree path. Add that PBI to the depends_on of PBI-007, so the deployment cannot land first; the areas of PBI-007 (local/deploy/**, local/tests/**) cannot make the fix. If that dependency cannot be recorded without the owner, treat this condition as unmet and escalate for a scope widening instead (disposition a). Do not make the change inside PBI-014 without an owner-approved scope change.

findings.title: For this project's own worktree builds the run detail gives only bare file names and tells the owner they are outside the project repository. That is wrong for about half of dispatch-board's recorded edits and every future worktree build, and the limitation is stated nowhere

evidence.value: A name after …/ is a file outside the project repository, its folders withheld. (Page text as written.)

dispatch-board: 65 of 140 edited-path occurrences are under C:/Users/jdk/dispatch-board-worktrees/<PBI>/, and all 65 publish as …/<name> although each is one of the project's own files. Another 56 are in the main checkout and publish repo-relative; 19 are genuinely elsewhere. platform-catalogue, edited in its main checkout: 110 publish repo-relative and 10 are outside. git worktree list shows PBI-007 and PBI-014 both in worktrees, so the worktree share only grows.

Of the 20 dispatch-board agents with worktree edits, only 4 recorded the worktree as their cwd; the rest recorded ~ or the main checkout. The claim that nothing in a transcript reliably ties a worktree to repoPath holds.

Paths are de-duplicated on the published name, so two different files in one worktree (site/index.html and local/static/index.html) collapse into a single …/index.html. The probe confirms this; no current run hits it.

0 of 37 code-reviewer runs (24 dispatch-board, 13 platform-catalogue) made an edit tool call, so for a reviewer the files line always falls back to Files its findings name. That fallback appears only when the result carried a findings block: live cache shows 11 of 24 for dispatch-board and 3 of 13 for platform-catalogue.

findings.impact: Files touched is delivered in substance for edits made in a main checkout (platform-catalogue, and dispatch-board's earlier builds). For worktree builds it gives only file names without folders, which is still useful, but the page's gloss actively misinforms by calling the project's own site/index.html a file outside the project repository. The AC-82 demonstration can pass honestly on a review round that carries a findings block plus a builder run. It would overstate the feature if the owner took the panel at face value for a worktree build.
findings.remediation: Before merge, in scope (site/** and tests/page.test.mjs): reword the …/ note so it cannot misdescribe a worktree. For example: a name after …/ was edited outside the project's main checkout, such as in a git worktree of it or elsewhere, its folders withheld. Pin the wording in the AC-82 page check. Either de-duplicate on the normalised source path before reducing to …/<name>, or state the collapse. At close-out, the AC-82 evidence should demonstrate on a review round with a findings block and on a builder run, and should state the worktree limitation plainly. Follow-up for the owner: let a project declare its worktree root (for example the <repoPath>-worktrees/<id>/ pattern) so worktree edits publish repo-relative. Do not use git worktree list, which forgets a removed worktree and would flip historical runs back to bare names.

findings.title: Files it edited lists every edit tool call, including calls the tool refused or that failed, and a home-relative or drive-relative path is published with its folders despite the folders-withheld rule

evidence.value: The path is appended on the tool_use record itself and the matching tool_result is never consulted, so a denied or failed Edit on a file that was never changed still appears under Files it edited.

Home-relative ~/.ssh/id_rsa publishes as ~/.ssh/id_rsa, and drive-relative C:foo/bar/baz.txt publishes as C:foo/bar/baz.txt, because both are treated as plain relative paths. Both inputs are reachable only through a call the Edit and Write tools reject for not being absolute.

No absolute path leaked for: another drive (D:); a UNC path in either slash direction; the extended-length form; mixed case against repoPath (c:/users/JDK/Dispatch-Board); repoPath itself with or without a trailing separator; <repo>/../x and deeper climbs; a sibling-prefix folder; an 8.3 short name; a trailing-dot folder; the Git Bash /c/ form. Every value reaches the page through esc() (site/index.html:597), and a scratch mutant with esc() removed fails the AC-82 check.

findings.impact: Low. Only the owner sees the board, a successful retry of a failed edit de-duplicates to the same file, and the folder leak needs input the tool itself refuses. The line can still name a file the run never changed, for example after a blocked-area or permission refusal.
findings.remediation: In publishable_files, treat a path starting with ~, or with a drive letter not followed by a slash, as outside the repository. Then either drop edits whose tool_result has is_error, or word the line as the files the run wrote to or tried to. Pin both cases in test_derive.py.

Not exercised on a real filesystem. publishable_files is purely lexical by design: a junction inside the repository that points outside publishes its in-repo relative name, and one outside that points in publishes as …/<name>. Neither publishes an absolute path, but the name can differ from the real target.
